title: Inverting the Transform
intro: Getting x[n] back from X(z) needs both the formula and the ring it is valid on. Partial fractions split the surface into one-pole pieces; the contour integral reads the answer off a circle inside the ring.

blocks.text: Partial fractions: one pole at a time
A rational $X(z)$ with distinct poles splits into simple pieces, each with one pole:

blocks.tex: X(z) = \sum_k \frac{A_k}{1 - p_k z^{-1}}, \qquad A_k = \left. \left(1 - p_k z^{-1}\right) X(z) \right|_{z = p_k}

blocks.text: (plus a polynomial in $z^{-1}$ if the numerator's degree is not lower than the denominator's). Each piece is one exponential, and the ROC decides which kind: if the ROC lies outside $p_k$, the piece is the right-sided $A_k p_k^n u[n]$; if inside, the left-sided $-A_k p_k^n u[-n-1]$.
The coefficients: $A_1 = 1/(1 - 0.25/0.5) = 2$ and $A_2 = 1/(1 - 0.5/0.25) = -1$. The poles at 0.25 and 0.5 allow three ROCs, and each gives a different signal:

items: $|z| > 0.5$, outside both poles: $x[n] = \left(2 \cdot 0.5^n - 0.25^n\right) u[n]$. Causal and stable.
$0.25 < |z| < 0.5$, between them: $x[n] = -2 \cdot 0.5^n u[-n-1] - 0.25^n u[n]$. Two-sided and unstable (the unit circle is outside the ring).
$|z| < 0.25$, inside both: $x[n] = \left(-2 \cdot 0.5^n + 0.25^n\right) u[-n-1]$. Left-sided and unstable.

blocks.text: The same surface, three signals: each answer corresponds to a different ring of it being the real one.

For a causal signal, dividing the numerator by the denominator as power series in $z^{-1}$ gives the samples one by one: the coefficient of $z^{-n}$ is $x[n]$. For $1/(1 - 0.5z^{-1})$ the division gives $1 + 0.5z^{-1} + 0.25z^{-2} + \cdots$, so $x[n] = 0.5^n$. It gives no closed form, but it is a quick check of the first few samples and works for any rational $X(z)$.
The contour integral: reading the answer off a circle
The general inverse comes from Cauchy's integral theorem. For any circle $\Gamma$ that lies in the ROC and goes once round the origin anticlockwise,

Geometrically, pick any ring of the surface that is real, walk round it, and average $X(z) z^n$ along the way. If the unit circle is in the ROC and $\Gamma$ is taken to be it, $z = e^{j\omega}$ and $dz = j e^{j\omega} d\omega$, and the integral becomes the inverse DTFT:

Because $X(z) z^{n-1}$ is analytic between the poles, the integral does not change as the circle is moved within the ring. It changes only when the circle is dragged across a pole, which is the contour-integral view of why each ROC gives a different signal. The residue theorem then evaluates it as the sum of the residues of $X(z) z^{n-1}$ at the poles inside $\Gamma$.

In the viewer the two-sided exponential has poles at $r$ and $1/r$ and the ring between them. A circle anywhere in that ring gives back $r^{|n|}$. For $n \ge 0$ the only pole inside the circle is $r$, and its residue gives the right-sided half. For $n < 0$ the factor $z^{n-1}$ adds a pole at the origin; the residues at 0 and $r$ together equal minus the residue at $1/r$, so the left-sided half can be read off the pole outside the circle.

blocks.title: Pick the ROC
blocks.text: $X(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 - 0.9 z^{-1}}$. Give $x[n]$ for the stable choice of ROC.
solution: The only pole is at 0.9. The stable ROC must contain the unit circle, so it is $|z| > 0.9$, and $x[n] = 0.9^n u[n]$.

blocks.title: Partial fractions
blocks.text: Find the causal $x[n]$ with $X(z) = \dfrac{3}{(1 - z^{-1})(1 + 0.5 z^{-1})}$.
solution: Causal means $|z| > 1$, so both pieces are right-sided: $x[n] = (2 + (-0.5)^n)\, u[n]$. Check: $x[0] = 3 = \lim_{z \to \infty} X(z)$.
